title: Acid Suppression and Esophageal Adenocarcinoma: A Critique of Causal Inference
content: This paper examines the inferential framework used to attribute the positive association between esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) and acid-suppressive therapy (AS) to confounding by indication. The experimental literature has proposed several hypotheses by which the use of AS may increase the risk of EAC, yet the clinical consensus is that the AS--EAC association reflects confounding by gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), a common indication for AS. This interpretation appears to be informed primarily by observational studies that attempt to isolate a GERD-independent component of the AS--EAC association and subsequently interpret their near-null estimates for this component as evidence against causality. These studies are among the most heavily cited in the AS--EAC literature, and their findings have been presented directly in clinician-facing works as reassuring evidence that the use of AS does not increase the risk of EAC, including in current clinical guidelines. After presenting several hypotheses discussed in the in vivo literature, this paper argues that these hypotheses each presuppose that the patient's underlying reflux burden is an effect modifier, and that the findings of these observational studies do not distinguish confounding by GERD from the causal mechanisms proposed in the in vivo literature. The paper concludes by discussing the broader epidemiologic evidence base and the unique challenges posed by this class of hypothesized causal structures.
